extracted.intended_audience: law students, patent practitioners, and inventors seeking practical guidance on PTO prosecution and post-issuance procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards governing U.S. patent application processing, examination, responses, appeals, continuing applications, post-allowance activity, interferences, and post-issuance corrections. Emphasizes formal requirements, timing, and substantive doctrines (e.g., enablement, new matter, priority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date and application numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: All papers arriving at the mail room of the PTO are stamped with the date of receipt ('filing date'). Any papers purporting to be a new application, whether complete or incomplete, are also stamped with an application number, which includes a two-digit 'series code' and a six-digit serial number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The series code is needed to identify an application unambiguously because serial numbers repeat over time; the PTO requires use of the full application number (series code + serial number).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial completeness and formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Application Division decides whether an application is complete and meets all formal requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings are forwarded to the official draftsman for compliance review; assignments are recorded by the Assignment Division and returned with reel/frame numbers; notices of informalities are placed in the file wrapper and must be corrected within times set by the examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of application
rubrics_metrics.description: The Application Division determines the appropriate PTO class and subclass for the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The classification determines the examining group to which the file is forwarded; classes and subclasses searched are noted on the file wrapper.

rubrics_metrics.name: §111 elements and clarity for examination
rubrics_metrics.description: When an application reaches an examining group, the examiner first ascertains that the application contains the four elements required by 35 U.S.C. § 111 and that it is clear enough to be examined, and whether it contains more than one invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the application is not sufficiently clear (e.g., filed by a foreign applicant not conforming to idiomatic English or U.S. practice), the examiner may request clarification (MPEP §702.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-invention requirement (restriction/election)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner determines the application contains more than one invention, the first Examiner's Action will list the inventions and include either a 'restriction requirement' (inventions clearly different) or an 'election of species requirement' (related inventions with a generic claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must choose one invention for prosecution; non-elected inventions under a restriction require divisional applications to pursue them; nonelected claims under an election may be rejoined if a generic claim is allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art search and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: After determining the application is examinable and single-invention, the examiner conducts a search for prior art relevant to the claimed subject matter and notes the classes/subclasses searched on the file wrapper. Documents found are called 'references.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search may be conducted in the examiner's private materials, the examining group's restricted library, or the PTO Scientific Library. The quality and thoroughness of the search depend on the examiner's searching skill, allotted time, and completeness of libraries searched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and contents of Examiner's Action (Office Action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Examiner's Action includes at least two parts: a form cover letter (examiner summarizes the action by checking boxes and filling blanks) and a typewritten explanation of the action; it may include itemized attachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically called 'Office Action'; attachments such as Notice of References Cited (PTO-892) or PTO-1449 (information disclosure) may be included and returned initialed by the examiner as evidence of consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of substantive Examiner actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The first substantive Examiner's Action can allow claims, reject claims, object to claims, object to the specification, or withdraw claims not elected for prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections commonly arise under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 (anticipation) and 103 (obviousness) and under §112 for indefiniteness; specification objections include nonenablement under §112 ('enablement' — must describe invention in full, clear terms enabling one skilled in the art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant response timing and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the period of time allotted for response (usually extendable up to a statutory maximum of six months upon payment of a fee), the applicant must respond to all of the examiner's rejections and objections or the application is abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses may include claim amendments, argument, affidavits (e.g., to establish prior invention or nonobviousness); failure to timely respond leads to abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible responses and evidentiary submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may respond to rejections and objections by amendment of the claims, by argument, or by a combination; responses may include affidavits as to nonobviousness or to establish invention prior to some reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are amended to overcome prior art, supporting the amended claim must be consistent with the original disclosure; affidavits can be used where appropriate to challenge prior art dates or obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on introducing 'new matter'
rubrics_metrics.description: In amending the application, particularly the specification, the applicant may not introduce 'new matter'—subject matter that was not in the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amending the specification to support an originally filed claim is acceptable; adding material not supported by the original disclosure to support an amendment is prohibited and can render the amendment impermissible (see In re Rasmussen, In re Winkhaus). Corrections of grammar or language (e.g., to non-idiomatic English) are generally permissible without introducing new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement standard for specification (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the invention 'in such full, clear, concise and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains . . . to make and use' it; otherwise, the specification may be objected to as nonenabling and claims directed to nonenabled subject matter are rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonenablement objections may preclude amending the specification to add support without introducing new matter; enablement is a substantive requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration and Notice of Allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: If, after applicant response, the examiner is satisfied, he or she issues a Notice of Allowance informing the applicant of allowance and setting a non-extendable three-month period to pay the issue fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice of Allowance may be accompanied by a Notice of Allowability and attachments (Examiner's Amendment, Notice of References Cited, initialed PTO-1449); drawing corrections held in abeyance may be reminded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Examiner's Action consequences and appeal timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: A second or subsequent Examiner's Action (unless based on a new ground) may be made 'final.' After a final action, while new amendments and arguments may be presented, the examiner is no longer required to consider them as of right; by six months from the date of the final Examiner's Action, the application must be allowed or an appeal filed, or it will be considered abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finality limits prosecution options and triggers appeal or continuing-application strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview rights and recordation
rubrics_metrics.description: From issuance of the first Examiner's Action until a final Examiner's Action, the applicant or representative is entitled to a personal or telephonic interview with the examiner to clarify issues and seek allowance; after final action, interviews are discretionary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must make the substance of the interview of record by completing an Examiner Interview Summary Record form; unless excused, the applicant must also file a summary of the interview (37 C.F.R. § 1.133(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responses after final action and entry of amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses filed after a final action are answered by a Notice of Allowance, Notice of Allowability, or an Advisory Action (form letter indicating why an amendment was not entered). An amendment may be refused entry if it raises 'new issues' or requires additional searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may enter an amendment only for purposes of an appeal; post-final practice is limited and subject to stricter scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Options after final rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: After a final rejection, the applicant may: abandon the application; file an appeal with the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences; take the allowed claims and cancel the others; or file a continuing application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic choice depends on the strengths of allowed vs. rejected claims and potential for continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal procedure and timing to Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant appeals, two months (extendable to six) are allowed to file an Appeal Brief; after filing, the examiner must file an Examiner's Answer (no statutory time limit); within one month of the Examiner's Answer the applicant may file a Reply Brief limited to new points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may request an oral hearing (generally filed within two months of Examiner's Answer but can be filed earlier); appeals are decided by a three-judge panel; board may affirm, reverse, or remand; outcomes affect further prosecution or allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing application requirements (claiming continuing status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for claiming continuing status: (1) application must be filed while the parent is still pending ('copendency'); (2) at least one inventor must be common to both applications; and (3) the text of the second application must refer back to the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A continuing application is entitled to the parent's filing date for subject matter contained in it; strategic uses include pursuing canceled or nonelected claims, presenting amendments/arguments not entered in parent, or adding new claiming approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and priority effects of continuation, continuation-in-part, divisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuation: same specification as parent, claims may differ, entitled to parent's filing date for subject matter contained in it. Continuation-in-part: shares some subject matter with parent and also adds new matter; entitled to parent's filing date only for common subject matter and to its own filing date for new matter. Divisional: a continuing application based on a parent with same specification but different claims (often due to restriction/election); entitled to parent's filing date for all purposes and protected from being used as prior art when division was made because of an examiner's requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary divisions that are actually continuations are not protected from prior-art effects of a patent issued on the earlier application; continuation-in-part may be filed to include new matter (e.g., improvements) as long as parent is still pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-allowance amendment and submission standards
rubrics_metrics.description: After Notice of Allowance, amendments can be made only upon a showing of good cause why they were not made earlier; submissions of additional prior art by applicant will only be considered if applicant certifies the art was not known to the applicant more than three months prior to submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments correcting Examiner's Amendment or non-substantive typographical corrections are usually entered if they do not change meaning; standards become stricter after payment of the issue fee as printing preparations begin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for withdrawal from issue after allowance/issue fee
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may be withdrawn from issue by the PTO or on petition by the applicant on showing good cause (e.g., discovery of new prior art). Once the issue fee is paid, a patent will be withdrawn from issue only for: (1) mistake on the part of the Office; (2) violation of 37 C.F.R. § 1.56 or illegality in the application; (3) unpatentability of one or more claims; (4) for interference; or (5) for abandonment to permit consideration of an information disclosure statement in a continuing application (37 C.F.R. § 1.313(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawal after issue fee is paid is constrained; typical good-cause justifications are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign priority (Paris Convention/GATT) and priority effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant can claim the benefit of a foreign filing date under the Paris Convention or (post-GATT) under 35 U.S.C. § 119(a–d) if the U.S. application is filed within one year of the first foreign filing; priority can be claimed anytime during pendency and is perfected by filing a certified copy of the foreign application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials published between the priority (foreign) date and the U.S. filing date are not prior art to the U.S. application for subject matter entitled to the priority date. However, the one-year period of 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) is counted from the earliest effective U.S. filing date, not from a foreign priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference declaration and standards (first-to-invent)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more applications claim the same subject matter, the examiner can declare an interference (or the applicant can provoke one). An interference determines which party was first to make the invention. 'Invention' for interference includes conception and reduction to practice (actual or constructive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities relied upon to establish invention must occur in the United States, a NAFTA country, or a GATT/WTO member; where one party conceived first but reduced to practice later, diligence between conception and reduction to practice may determine priority (35 U.S.C. § 102(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protest and public use proceedings (third-party challenges)
rubrics_metrics.description: A protest is a paper submitted by a third party citing prior art and explaining why that art should prevent issuance of a patent; the protester is not given further opportunity to communicate and is not informed of later prosecution unless the examiner requires applicant response. A public use proceeding addresses prior art consisting of public use or sale (by applicant/assignee or others) and may be inter partes in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use proceedings involve testimony and exchange of briefs and may include an oral hearing if inter partes; examiner's decision in a public use proceeding is not appealable unless it forms the basis of a rejection (37 C.F.R. §§ 1.291, 1.292).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office of Quality Review sampling and reexamination
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO's Office of Quality Review randomly selects a predetermined number of allowed applications from each art unit for review; selected applications already reviewed by the Board or a court are excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentability review examiner reexamines the file and may perform an independent prior-art search; questions may be returned to the originating group director who may resolve them or refer to a panel (original examiner, review examiner, supervisory primary examiner, director of quality review, and group director). If warranted, allowance may be rescinded and prosecution reopened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial appeal options from PTO decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant dissatisfied with a Board decision may initiate a civil action against the Commissioner in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (trial de novo). Appeals from the district court go exclusively to the Federal Circuit; alternatively, an applicant may appeal directly from the PTO to the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice most appeals are taken directly to the Federal Circuit; Federal Circuit decisions are subject to Supreme Court certiorari review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers, dedications, and terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent owner may disclaim or dedicate to the public the entire term of an entire patent, the entire term of any complete claim, or the terminal part of the term of the entire patent. Terminal disclaimers may be used to avoid 'double patenting' and cause patents to expire on the same day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers require payment of a fee set by regulation, publication in the Official Gazette, and printed copies for attachment to patents; terminal disclaimers are effective only for obviousness-type double patenting (35 U.S.C. § 253; 37 C.F.R. § 1.321).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates of Correction and correction of inventorship
rubrics_metrics.description: If printing errors arise in the printing of a patent, the PTO must issue a certificate under seal stating the nature of the errors and attach a copy to each printed patent. An applicant may obtain a Certificate of Correction for clerical or typographical errors for which the applicant was responsible if the error was made in good faith. The PTO will also issue a certificate correcting inventorship either by court order or petition by the patent owner, provided the error in naming inventors was made in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certificates of Correction issued by the PTO are published in the Official Gazette and the corrected patent and certificate together have the same effect as if the patent had been issued correctly; applicant-paid certificates require a fee and good-faith showing.
